nodes.summary: Let $h$ and $h_f$ be disjoint heaps, $c$ a heap command and $s$ a store, and suppose that the configuration $(c, s, h)$ can take a small step. If $(c, s, h \cup h_f)$ takes a small step to $(c', s', h'')$, then there is a heap $h_1$, disjoint from $h_f$, such that $(c, s, h)$ takes a small step to $(c', s', h_1)$ and $h'' = h_1 \cup h_f$.
nodes.title: Frame decomposition of a single heap step

nodes.summary: Let $h$ and $h_f$ be disjoint heaps, $c$ a heap command and $s$ a store, and suppose that the configuration $(c, s, h)$ is safe. If $(c, s, h \cup h_f)$ reaches $(c'', s'', h'')$ by finitely many (possibly zero) small steps, then there is a heap $h_2$, disjoint from $h_f$, such that $(c, s, h)$ reaches $(c'', s'', h_2)$ by finitely many small steps, $h'' = h_2 \cup h_f$, and $(c'', s'', h_2)$ is safe.
nodes.title: Frame decomposition of heap executions

nodes.summary: For every heap $h$, the empty heap is disjoint from $h$ (with the empty heap as the first heap).
nodes.title: The empty heap is disjoint from every heap

nodes.summary: For every heap $h$, $h$ is disjoint from the empty heap (with the empty heap as the second heap).
nodes.title: Every heap is disjoint from the empty heap

nodes.summary: If heaps $h_1$ and $h_2$ are disjoint, then for every address $a$, the heap obtained from $h_1$ by erasing $a$ (removing the address $a$ and its value) is disjoint from $h_2$.
nodes.title: Erasing an address preserves disjointness

nodes.summary: If heaps $h_1$ and $h_2$ are disjoint and the address $a$ is not allocated in $h_2$, then for every value $v$, the heap obtained from $h_1$ by inserting $a$ with value $v$ (overwriting any value $h_1$ stores at $a$) is disjoint from $h_2$.
nodes.title: Inserting an address the other heap lacks preserves disjointness

nodes.summary: For every address $a$, value $v$ and heap $h$, the singleton heap that stores $v$ at $a$ and allocates no other address is disjoint from $h$ if and only if $a$ is not allocated in $h$.
nodes.title: Disjointness from a singleton heap

nodes.summary: Two heaps $h_1$ and $h_2$ are disjoint when no address is allocated in both: every address allocated in $h_1$ is not allocated in $h_2$.
nodes.title: Disjoint heaps

nodes.summary: For heaps $h_1$ and $h_2$, let $h_1 \cup h_2$ be their left-biased union (at an address allocated in both it keeps the value from $h_1$). If the address $a$ is not allocated in $h_2$, then erasing $a$ from $h_1 \cup h_2$ gives the union of $h_2$ with the heap obtained from $h_1$ by erasing $a$, taken with that heap on the left.
nodes.title: Erasing an address that the right heap of a union lacks

nodes.summary: For every heap $h$ there is an address that is not allocated in $h$.
nodes.title: Every heap has a free address

nodes.summary: Let $h$ and $h_f$ be disjoint heaps, $c$ a heap command and $s$ a store. If the configuration $(c, s, h)$ can take a small step, then so can $(c, s, h \cup h_f)$.
nodes.title: Adding a frame heap preserves the ability to step

nodes.summary: A heap configuration is a triple $(c, s, h)$ of a heap command $c$, a store $s$ and a heap $h$.
nodes.title: Heap configurations

nodes.summary: Heap commands extend the commands of IMP with heap operations. A heap command is one of: $\mathbf{skip}$; an assignment $x := a$; a sequence $c_1; c_2$; a conditional $\mathbf{if}\ b\ \mathbf{then}\ c_1\ \mathbf{else}\ c_2$; a loop $\mathbf{while}\ b\ \mathbf{do}\ c$; a heap read $x := [a]$; a heap write $[a] := e$; an allocation $x := \mathbf{alloc}(e)$; or a deallocation $\mathbf{free}(a)$. Here $x$ is a variable…
nodes.title: Heap commands

nodes.summary: A heap is a finite partial map from addresses to values, where addresses and values are natural numbers: it stores a value $v \in \mathbb{N}$ at each address of a finite set of addresses in $\mathbb{N}$, called the addresses allocated in the heap.
nodes.title: Heap

nodes.summary: The single-step relation $(c, s, h) \to (c', s', h')$ on heap configurations is the least relation closed under the rules below. Here $a(s)$ is the value of an expression $a$ in the store $s$, $s[x \mapsto n]$ is $s$ with variable $x$ set to $n$, $h[\ell \mapsto n]$ is $h$ with address $\ell$ set to $n$, and $h \setminus \ell$ is $h$ with address $\ell$ removed.
nodes.title: Small-step semantics of heap commands

nodes.summary: The relation $(c, s, h) \to^* (c', s', h')$ on heap configurations is the reflexive-transitive closure of the small-step relation: it holds when the first configuration reaches the second by a finite, possibly empty, sequence of small steps.
nodes.title: Multi-step heap execution

nodes.summary: If a heap $h$ stores the value $v$ at the address $a$, then erasing $a$ from $h$ and then inserting $a$ with value $v$ gives back $h$.
nodes.title: Reinserting an erased value restores the heap

nodes.summary: Write $\mathrm{mod}(c)$ for the set of variables a heap command $c$ may assign to. If the configuration $(c, s, h)$ takes a small step to $(c', s', h')$, then $\mathrm{mod}(c') \subseteq \mathrm{mod}(c)$.
nodes.title: Steps do not enlarge the modified variables

nodes.summary: The set $\mathrm{mod}(c)$ of variables a heap command $c$ may assign to is defined by recursion on $c$. It is empty for $\mathbf{skip}$, a heap write $[a] := e$ and a deallocation $\mathbf{free}(a)$; it is $\{x\}$ for an assignment $x := a$, a heap read $x := [a]$ and an allocation $x := \mathbf{alloc}(e)$; it is $\mathrm{mod}(c_1) \cup \mathrm{mod}(c_2)$ for a sequence $c_1; c_2$ and for a conditional…
nodes.title: Modified variables of a heap command

nodes.summary: If a heap configuration is safe and reaches a second configuration by finitely many (possibly zero) small steps, then the second configuration is safe.
nodes.title: Safety is preserved along executions

nodes.summary: Let $c$ be a plain IMP command, $s$ a store and $h$ a heap, and write $\overline{d}$ for the embedding of a plain command $d$ into the heap language. If $(\overline{c}, s, h)$ reaches a heap configuration $(c_2, s_2, h_2)$ in zero or more heap steps, then $h_2 = h$ and there is a plain command $c_2'$ with $c_2 = \overline{c_2'}$ such that $(c, s)$ reaches $(c_2', s_2)$ in zero or more plain small steps.
nodes.title: Executions of embedded commands are plain executions

nodes.summary: For every plain IMP command $c$ with embedding $\overline{c}$ into the heap language, every store $s$ and every heap $h$, the heap configuration $(\overline{c}, s, h)$ is safe.
nodes.title: Embedded plain commands are safe

nodes.summary: A heap configuration, consisting of a heap command, a store and a heap, is safe when every heap configuration reachable from it in zero or more heap steps either has command $\mathtt{skip}$ or can take a further heap step.
nodes.title: Safe heap configurations

nodes.summary: If a heap configuration $(c, s, h)$ reaches a heap configuration $(c', s', h')$ in zero or more heap steps, then $s'(x) = s(x)$ for every variable $x$ outside the set of variables that $c$ may assign to.
nodes.title: Heap executions only change assignable variables

nodes.summary: If a heap configuration $(c, s, h)$ takes one heap step to $(c', s', h')$, then $s'(x) = s(x)$ for every variable $x$ outside the set of variables that $c$ may assign to.
nodes.title: A heap step only changes assignable variables

nodes.summary: For heaps $h_1$ and $h_2$, if $h_1$ and $h_2$ are disjoint, then $h_2$ and $h_1$ are disjoint.
nodes.title: Symmetry of heap disjointness

nodes.summary: Let $c$ be a plain IMP command with embedding $\overline{c}$ into the heap language, let $s, s'$ be stores and let $h$ be a heap. Then $c$ terminates from $s$ with final store $s'$ if and only if $(\overline{c}, s, h)$ reaches $(\mathtt{skip}, s', h)$ in zero or more heap steps.
nodes.title: Embedding preserves termination

nodes.summary: Let $c$ be a plain IMP command, $s$ a store and $h$ a heap, and write $\overline{d}$ for the embedding of a plain command $d$ into the heap language. Then $(\overline{c}, s, h)$ takes a heap step to a heap configuration $K$ if and only if there are a plain command $c'$ and a store $s'$ such that $(c, s)$ takes a plain small step to $(c', s')$ and $K = (\overline{c'}, s', h)$.
nodes.title: Heap steps of embedded commands are plain steps

nodes.summary: Let $c, c_2$ be plain IMP commands, $s, s_2$ stores and $h$ a heap, and write $\overline{d}$ for the embedding of a plain command $d$ into the heap language. If $(c, s)$ reaches $(c_2, s_2)$ in zero or more plain small steps, then $(\overline{c}, s, h)$ reaches $(\overline{c_2}, s_2, h)$ in zero or more heap steps.
nodes.title: Plain executions lift to the heap language

nodes.summary: The embedding sends each plain IMP command to the heap command of the same shape: $\mathtt{skip}$ goes to $\mathtt{skip}$, an assignment of an arithmetic expression to a variable goes to the same assignment, a sequence goes to the sequence of the embeddings of its parts, and a conditional or while loop goes to the conditional or while loop with the same guard and with each subcommand replaced by its embedding.
nodes.title: Embedding of IMP into the heap language

can_prove.label: ready to prove
can_prove.meaning: Statement is in Lean and nothing it needs is blocked, so the proof can start.

can_state.label: ready to state
can_state.meaning: Everything its statement uses is in Lean, so the statement can be written in Lean.

conditional.label: conditionally proved
conditional.meaning: Proof compiles, but rests on an open statement without a recorded Lean proof.

fully_proved.label: fully proved
fully_proved.meaning: Proved, and every prerequisite is fully proved too.

inventory_checked.label: inventory checked
inventory_checked.meaning: Module inventory checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

inventory_pending.label: inventory pending
inventory_pending.meaning: Module inventory not yet checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

not_ready.label: not ready
not_ready.meaning: Needs more blueprint work before it can be attempted.

proved.label: proved
proved.meaning: Proof compiles, but something it rests on is not finished.

stated.label: statement formalized
stated.meaning: Statement is in Lean; the proof is not.
